FLASHCARD SET · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Playground flashcards.

Thirty-two cards from the school’s Playground: the words our bodies do there — balance, jump, swing — the things on the ground, from the ball to the tunnel, and the five manners that make play work together. Every card carries its picture word, the words to say together and one game — the whole playground, ready to print.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    Playground word hunt

    Take three cards to the real playground and hunt the words live — run on the path, the real slide, the real bench. Saying the word while the body does it sticks twice as deep.

  2. 02

    Do the word

    Pick a card and do it in the living room: jump, balance on a tape line, push a box. The picture word becomes the instruction — and your child becomes the game show host.

  3. 03

    Manners rehearsal

    Before the playground, play the five manners as a quick story: someone wants the swing — what do we do? Help, share, stop, take turns, wait — five cards, five answers, one calm trip out.

  4. 04

    Card treasure drop

    Hide four cards around the playground (or the flat), find them and DO each word on the spot. Finding plus doing is the whole set in one round of giggles.

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Balance Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Balance — holding steady when everything wants to wobble. One foot, a kerb, a low bench: the whole body goes quiet and listens to itself. This card turns any edge at the playground into a tightrope.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Balance means staying steady on your feet. It happens in your ears, your eyes and your legs all at once — three helpers checking in with each other so you do not tip.

      How do you do it?

      Pick a line — a kerb, a bench edge, chalk on the path. Walk it slowly, arms out like airplane wings. The slower you go, the steadier you get.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Balancing is quiet, focused body work. It asks a child to slow down, look ahead and feel their own middle — a deep breath disguised as a game.

      Say it together

      “Arms out, eyes forward — step… step… steady! Balance is your body talking to itself, and you are the boss of it.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Tape a line on the floor and walk it forwards, backwards and sideways. Then try it with a beanbag on your head and see how far Mr. Beanbag rides along.

      Quick parent note

      Wobbling is the lesson, not the failure. Every wobble is the body practising its comeback — count the wobbles together and watch them shrink.

      Teach it, step by step

      This card belongs to a real class — open the The Playground class on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Catch Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Catch — two hands, one flying ball and one delicious moment of waiting. This card is the game every ball wants to play: watching with your whole body, then closing your hands at exactly the right beat.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Catch means stopping something that is moving through the air by holding it with your hands. Your eyes do the hard part first — they follow the ball and tell your hands where to be.

      How do you do it?

      Stand face to face, a big step apart. The thrower says the magic words — “ready… go!” — and the catcher keeps eyes on the ball until it lands in their hands.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Catching trains the eyes and the hands to work as a team. It is also a two-person game, so every catch carries a little conversation with it: my turn to throw, your turn to shine.

      Say it together

      “Ready… watch the ball… now! Catch! Two hands close like a bird cage around the ball.”

      Try this

      Start with a big, soft beach ball hugged against the chest. Step back one tiny step for every catch. Ten catches in a row earns a silly victory dance.

      Quick parent note

      If catching will not click today, roll the ball instead. Catching on the ground is the same skill wearing training wheels, and it counts.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Climb Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Climb — up, on purpose. Hands grab, feet push, and the world gets higher one hold at a time. This card is for every child who sees a climbing wall and feels their arms tingling.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Climb means moving upwards using your hands and feet together. Hands pull, feet push — that is the whole secret, and the arms do less work than children expect.

      How do you do it?

      On a climbing wall or frame, look first and plan the route out loud: “this bump for my hand, that one for my foot.” Climb only as high as feels brave today.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Climbing is planning with your whole body. Each hold is a small decision — left or right, reach or step — and reaching the top is a confidence a child can feel in their shoulders.

      Say it together

      “Hand, hand, foot, foot — up we go! Climb means your hands and feet are friends and they take turns.”

      Try this

      Play “sticky hands” on the stairs at home: hands on the steps too — hands, feet, hands, feet, slowly, like a puppy. Same skill, indoors, zero height.

      Quick parent note

      Stand behind, not above. A spotter’s hand hovering near the back says “I am here” without stealing the climb.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Dig Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Dig — the sandbox’s own word. Spade in, sand out, and is that a hole or a tunnel or a road to the sea? This card belongs to every child who has ever lost track of time in a sandpit.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Dig means moving earth, sand or snow with a spade, your hands or something scoop-shaped. It is a pushing-and-lifting word with a treasure-hunting heart.

      How do you do it?

      Kneel by the sand, grip the spade with two hands and press down with your foot for extra power. Fill the bucket, tip it out, repeat — that is the whole job, and it never gets old.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Digging is real resistance work — the sand pushes back, and the arms and shoulders grow stronger every scoop. It is also open-ended: one hole can be a swimming pool, a dinosaur home or a well.

      Say it together

      “Scoop and sprinkle, scoop and sprinkle — dig, dig, dig! What will we find under the sand today?”

      Try this

      Bury a treasure (a big spoon, a toy, a shiny stone) and dig it up again. Bury it deeper each time and listen to the effort grow.

      Quick parent note

      Wet sand digs differently to dry sand — one holds shapes, one runs away. That is early science happening under the fingernails.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Hide Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Hide — the word that starts a thousand giggles. Behind the panel, under the slide, inside the tunnel: hide is the half of hide-and-seek that children love best. Finding comes later.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Hide means putting yourself where nobody can see you. A good hiding spot needs a think first: what blocks my friend’s eyes from here?

      How do you do it?

      Pick a spot, fold yourself into it and stay quiet while the seeker counts. The counting voice is the clock — when it stops, the seeking begins.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Hiding is a perspective puzzle — children work out what another person can and cannot see. That skill has a grown-up name and a toddler name: peek-a-boo, level three.

      Say it together

      “One, two, three… where ARE you? Hide means quiet feet and a held breath and a grin you hope nobody sees.”

      Try this

      Hide a toy instead of a person first. Hide it badly on purpose — a tail sticking out — and let your child gloat. Then let them hide it for you.

      Quick parent note

      Some children hide and then worry when nobody finds them fast. Agree on a comeback whistle or word before the game starts.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Jump Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Jump — both feet leave the ground and for one bright moment gravity lets go. Off a step, over a puddle, down from the bottom rung: this card is pure joy with a landing.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Jump means pushing off the ground with both feet and coming back down. The secret ingredient is the bend before it — knees crouch like springs, then let go.

      How do you do it?

      Bend, swing your arms back, then throw them forward as your legs push. Land on two flat feet with soft knees — “land like a frog, not like a statue.”

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Jumping builds the biggest muscles in the body and the biggest feelings too — the first real jump is usually followed by ten more and one proud announcement: “DID YOU SEE THAT?”

      Say it together

      “Bend your knees… wiggle… JUMP! Both feet up, both feet down, land like a cat with bendy knees.”

      Try this

      Chalk two lines on the path and jump between them, then widen the river one shoe-length at a time. How wide can the crocodile river get before the jumping fails?

      Quick parent note

      Landing is the skill worth teaching first. Soft landings make brave jumpers — and keep ankles, floors and furniture friends.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Kick Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Kick — one swing of the leg and the ball goes flying. This card is for the smallest strikers: the ones who run at the ball, connect with a satisfying THUMP and chase it laughing.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Kick means hitting something with your foot to make it move. The standing foot points where you want the ball to go — the body aims before the kick fires.

      How do you do it?

      Put the ball still on the ground, stand close, plant the non-kicking foot beside it and swing. A slow kick that connects beats a mighty kick that finds air.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Kicking asks one leg to balance while the other works — that is a whole-body conversation. It also makes the ball obey: kick left, ball goes left. Cause and effect with a score line.

      Say it together

      “Plant your foot next to the ball, swing the other one — WHACK! Kick means one leg says hello to the ball, hard.”

      Try this

      Kick a balloon first — it hangs in the air long enough to feel successful. Then a soft ball, then a real one, and finally set up two shoes as a goal and shoot.

      Quick parent note

      Hold hands and kick together for the very first ones — your leg swings, their leg swings, the ball moves, the cheer is shared.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Play Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Play — the word the whole playground is built on. Arms wide, legs going, grin switched on: this card is the umbrella over every other card in the set.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Play means doing something for the fun of it — with your body, your voice, your imagination or a friend. Nobody has to play; that is exactly why it works.

      How do you do it?

      However the day allows. Ten minutes with two sticks is play. A made-up game in the queue at the shop is play. The card just gives the feeling a name.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Play is how children rehearse everything — language, turns, rules, courage. A child deep in play is not taking a break from learning; that IS the learning, wearing its favourite shoes.

      Say it together

      “Play is what we do when nobody is telling us what to do — running, pretending, building, giggling, again again again!”

      Try this

      Ask “what are we playing?” and then join the game by its own rules — if the floor is lava, your feet are in terrible danger. Follow the leader your child appoints.

      Quick parent note

      Boredom is play’s front door. Resist filling every empty minute — the best games start two minutes after “I have nothing to do-oo.”

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Pull Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Pull — the wagon word. Lean back, grip tight and the load comes along. This card is the satisfying half of tug: bringing something towards you, one strong step at a time.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Pull means bringing something closer by dragging or tugging it towards you. Your body leans away from the load — that lean is the trick that makes pulling easier than it looks.

      How do you do it?

      Two hands on the rope or handle, one foot back, body leaning away. Small strong steps work better than one giant heave — pull is a rhythm, not a jolt.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Pulling teaches weight — a wagon with one toy glides, a wagon with ten friends needs a plan. Children feel exactly how heavy “too much” is, and how to fix it: take something out.

      Say it together

      “Lean back and heave — pull, pull, PULL! The wagon follows the person who pulls it, like a duckling on wheels.”

      Try this

      Load a laundry basket with toys, tie a rope on and make it a train with stations. The passenger load decides whether the engine glides or groans.

      Quick parent note

      Pull games have a natural stop signal: rope down. Teach it before the tug-of-war era begins.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Push Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Push — the roundabout word. Hands flat, legs driving, and the whole thing spins faster. This card is giving: your push becomes somebody else’s ride.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Push means pressing something away from you to make it move. Pushing is the opposite of pulling — the load travels out, your hands stay behind it.

      How do you do it?

      Low hands, bent knees and push through the legs, not just the arms. Watch the rider’s face — push enough for giggles, not enough for wobbles.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Pushing a friend on a roundabout is physics and kindness in one job: too soft is boring, too hard is scary, and finding “just right” is a child reading another person — the root of empathy.

      Say it together

      “Hands on, bend your legs, PUSH! The roundabout only goes because someone pushes it — today that someone is you.”

      Try this

      Push games indoors: push a box of books across the rug, push your grown-up (gently!), push the shopping trolley. Heavy things make honest pushes.

      Quick parent note

      Roundabouts have rules — feet on, hands off when it spins. Say the rule as a cheer, not a warning: “feet on, hands round!”

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Run Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Run — the fastest word in the set. Heels drumming, hair bouncing, wind doing its thing. Every playground has one rule older than the fences: you do not have to run, but you will.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Run means moving so fast that for a moment both feet leave the ground between steps. That little flight is the difference a child feels instantly: walking never floats.

      How do you do it?

      Look ahead, not down. Arms pump like small engines, feet land softly. Start slow, finish fast — running away from a giggling grown-up is the classic training plan.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Running is the body’s big engine warming up — heart, lungs and legs all at once. It also burns off the wiggles that make sitting still hard, which is why a good run comes before a good puzzle.

      Say it together

      “Quick feet, elbows in — run, run, run! Running is walking that got exciting.”

      Try this

      Play “red light, green light” or race to the tree and back. Short sprints with a finish line teach more than long chases — and the finish line is where the laughing happens.

      Quick parent note

      Chase games need a safe rule: we stop when someone says STOP. Practise the stop as part of the game, so the brakes exist before the hill does.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Sit Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Sit — the bench word. Legs fold, body settles, and the playground slows down for a minute. This card is the rest stop between the running and the running.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Sit means resting your weight on your bottom, on a bench, a step or the ground. It is the word that turns a body from go to paused.

      How do you do it?

      Find a bench, turn around, lower down slow — no dropping like a sack. Feet flat or legs crossed, hands resting. Sitting well is a small skill with a big payoff.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Sitting on purpose — choosing to stop — is a bigger feat than it sounds. The bench is where snack happens, where friends get talked to, where the roundabout queue makes sense.

      Say it together

      “Bottom down, legs crossed — sit! Sitting is how your body takes a drink of quiet.”

      Try this

      Make the bench a shop, a bus or a pirate look-out. Sitting that has a story in it lasts twice as long as sitting that is just sitting.

      Quick parent note

      If sitting still is hard today, let the feet keep a quiet job — tapping a rhythm or squeezing a ball. Busy feet often make a calm top half.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Slide Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Slide — climb up, sit down, whoosh. The playground’s own rollercoaster, and the word every child learns on day one. This card is the two-second ride that gets repeated forty times.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Slide means moving smoothly down a sloped surface. On the slide, your legs provide the launch and gravity does the rest — a perfect teamwork of you and physics.

      How do you do it?

      Climb the ladder, turn around and sit before you go — feet first, one at a time, then scoot. The sliding rule is short and firm: feet always lead.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Sliding is a gentle risk with a built-in reward. The little flutter at the top, the whoosh, the safe landing — that cycle is how children learn that nervous and fun can live in the same body.

      Say it together

      “Up the steps, sit, feet first — WHEEE! Slide means the playground does the moving and you do the laughing.”

      Try this

      Slide counting: how many times can you slide before your legs get wobbly? Count out loud together — the number will be higher than you fear.

      Quick parent note

      Wet slides are fast slides. One hand on the way down keeps a slick ride from becoming a launch.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Swing Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Swing — back and forth, back and forth, higher with every go. This card is the rhythm word: legs pump, tummy floats, and the wind gets a turn to talk.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Swing means riding back and forth while hanging from something above. The swing moves because you move — legs pump out and tuck in, and the seat becomes a pendulum.

      How do you do it?

      Sit deep in the seat, hold on with both hands, lean back and push the legs out as you go forward, tuck them under as you come back. Small pumps, big arc — the rhythm does the work.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Swinging is rhythm and float in one motion — the tummy-drop feeling is the body learning about momentum, and pumping the legs is coordination wearing a party dress.

      Say it together

      “Lean back, legs out… tuck them in… swing! The legs are the engine and the sky is the destination.”

      Try this

      Behind-push first, then teach pumping with a rhyme: “out like a frog, in like a mouse.” One rhyme, one pump, and one day the pushes stop being needed.

      Quick parent note

      The request “push me higher” has a ceiling only the pusher can feel. Keep the arc that keeps the seat flat — giggles travel, seats should not.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Walk Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Walk — the get-there word. One foot, other foot, repeat until arrival. Slower than running, steadier than skipping, and the only way to carry an ice cream anywhere.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Walk means moving on your feet at a steady, manageable pace — one foot always on the ground. It is the body’s everyday speed, and children get to choose it.

      How do you do it?

      Eyes up, shoulders easy, feet rolling from heel to toe. Walk a line, walk a circle, walk backwards — same word, four games.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Walking is the pace where talking happens. Most of the day’s best conversations with a small child arrive at walking speed, midway between one interesting crack in the path and the next.

      Say it together

      “Heel, toe, heel, toe — walk! Walking is just falling forwards and catching yourself, over and over, on purpose.”

      Try this

      Walk home the slow way and let your child lead. Every twenty steps they pick the next turn — the map goes silly, the walking never notices.

      Quick parent note

      “Walk, please” works better with a job attached: “walk me to the gate and count the dogs.” A mission beats a command every time.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Ball Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A ball — the playground’s most patient toy. Round, bouncy and always ready: one ball is catch, football, ten-pin bowling and a picnic of games waiting to be chosen.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A ball is a round toy that rolls and bounces. Big soft balls are gentle for catching, small bouncy balls are cheeky for chasing — every size starts a different game.

      What is it like on the playground?

      The ball is the playground’s invitation: roll it to a friend and a game starts by itself. It never runs out of turns and it never picks teams badly.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Ball play sneaks in the whole curriculum — rolling is physics, catching is eye-teamwork, waiting is patience, and inventing rules is language. One ball, many lessons, zero worksheets.

      Say it together

      “Round and ready — a ball never says no. Bounce it, roll it, kick it, hug it: the ball plays whatever game you bring.”

      Try this

      Roll the ball back and forth sitting down, then bounce it standing, then kick it running. Same ball, three difficulties — your child picks the level.

      Quick parent note

      The beach ball in this picture is the best first ball: big, light and slow in the air. Small rubber balls come later, when the hands have caught a few victories.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Bench Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A bench — where the playground sits down. Snack base, shoe-change station, pirate ship, shop counter: the humble bench holds more games than anything bolted down.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A bench is a long seat with legs, built for more than one bottom at a time. This one is painted red, yellow and green — the playground’s own rainbow.

      What is it like on the playground?

      Benches are the quiet furniture: the meeting spot, the watch-the-big-kids spot, the “my legs need a minute” spot. Every playground story has a bench in it somewhere.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      A bench teaches rest as part of play — stop when the body asks, watch the game, go back when ready. Children who can sit and watch are learning the game twice: once with legs, once with eyes.

      Say it together

      “The bench is waiting — sit, snack, chat, go again. It is the playground’s kitchen table with the best view.”

      Try this

      Bench games: shopkeeper behind the counter, bus driver on the route, audience for the show. One bench, three careers.

      Quick parent note

      Benches are also where the best grown-up conversations happen. Sit at their level — the chat goes longer and stranger.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Climbing Frame Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A climbing frame — a jungle gym of bars and rails built for going up, over and across. The card says CLIMB, and that is the whole invitation: hands and feet, off you go.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A climbing frame is a frame of bars and poles you can climb on, hang from and cross over. This one is a dome of red, yellow and blue — half ladder, half maze.

      What is it like on the playground?

      You choose a route: over the top, through the middle or across the bars like a monkey. The frame does not mind which way — it is the same mountain either way.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Climbing frames are decision machines: which bar, which hand, how high today. Every crossing is planned, tried and finished by the climber — ownership you can see in the walk to the next challenge.

      Say it together

      “Grab the bars, find your feet — the climbing frame is a mountain that waits for small climbers and claps when they cross.”

      Try this

      Play “the floor is water” under the frame — feet stay on the bars. Then cross it three ways and pick a favourite route to show a friend.

      Quick parent note

      Busy frame, simple rule: one direction at a time. Keep your eyes on the climber, not the phone — tops of frames deserve a witness.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Fence Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A fence — the playground’s friendly border. Red, yellow and green posts standing in a row: the fence is where the playground says “this much, and no further” without ever sounding bossy.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A fence is a row of posts and rails that marks an edge. It does not move, it does not play, and that is its job: it keeps the game where the ground is soft.

      What is it like on the playground?

      The fence is the finish line of every race, the goal post of every kicking game and the spot where balls come to be rescued. It also tells you exactly where the gate is.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Edges make children feel safe enough to be wild. A clear boundary means the inside is predictable — and a predictable inside is where the biggest running happens.

      Say it together

      “The fence holds the playground like a hug — inside it, the running goes wild; outside it, the road does road things.”

      Try this

      Fence games: touch-the-fence tag (the fence is base), “what colour is your post?”, and counting the posts on the walk out. The border becomes a landmark.

      Quick parent note

      Fences are also the waiting spot for siblings and scooters. A pocket snack near the fence extends the playground day by twenty peaceful minutes.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Ladder Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A ladder — rung by rung, up you go. The ladder is the polite start of every big thing on the playground: the slide, the platform, the view from the top.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A ladder is two rails with rungs between them for climbing. Playground ladders stand still and lean on nothing — they are built into the climbing frame itself.

      What is it like on the playground?

      Up the ladder, over the platform, down the slide — the ladder is the first chapter of that story. Hands hold a rung, feet follow, and the turns repeat like a rhythm.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Ladders teach the hands-and-feet take-turns pattern that all climbing uses. They also teach a brave habit: pause on a rung, look where the foot goes next, then move.

      Say it together

      “One rung, two rung — hands and feet take turns. The ladder says: slow is fine, steady is better, the top is patient.”

      Try this

      Chalk a ladder on the pavement and hop it — two feet in each space, then one. Same climbing rhythm, ground floor, no height.

      Quick parent note

      Teach the ladder trick early: three points on at all times — two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand. It sounds grown-up; small climbers adopt it instantly.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Monkey Bars Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Monkey bars — a ceiling of bars you cross hand over hand, feet swinging below. The first crossing feels like a circus act, and it is: strength, grip and nerve in one shiny row.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      Monkey bars are a row of overhead bars you cross without touching the ground. This set is yellow and blue, and every bar is a small step of the journey.

      What is it like on the playground?

      Start at one end, reach for the next bar, then the next. Feet can help at first — hook a knee or let them dangle like the monkeys the bars are named for.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Crossing monkey bars builds grip and shoulder strength — real, useful, feel-it-tomorrow strength. They also build the habit of finishing: mid-bar is a bad place to quit, so children learn to commit.

      Say it together

      “Hand, hand, hand — swing across! The monkey bars ask your arms to be brave and your legs to just hang out.”

      Try this

      Build a home version with a sturdy broom held between two grown-ups. Three bars of practice at home make the playground row feel familiar.

      Quick parent note

      Falling from bars is part of the plot — teach the drop-and-bend: let go, land on two feet, knees soft. Kids who know how to fall off try more things.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Sandbox Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A sandbox — a square of beach in the middle of the playground. Bring a spade, bring a bucket, bring a story: the sand holds its shape just long enough for the idea to be built.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A sandbox is a big box, usually wooden and painted red and blue here, filled with sand for digging and building. It is the playground’s ingredient section.

      What is it like on the playground?

      One corner digs holes, another builds mountains, a third runs a bakery of sand pies. The sandbox fits every game at once because sand is whatever the hands say it is.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Sand is the best open-ended material on the playground — dry it runs, wet it builds, and in between it teaches almost-firm, almost-falling-apart. Measuring, pouring and sharing tools is early maths wearing a bucket.

      Say it together

      “Shoes off (or not) — the sandbox is open! Scoop, pour, pat, repeat: the sand never says the game is over.”

      Try this

      Bury a row of “gems” (bottle caps) and dig for treasure by number: “find four!” Scooping to an exact count is a sneaky maths lesson.

      Quick parent note

      Sandbox etiquette is simple and teachable: sand stays low (no tossing), tools go back, and the sand stays in the box — not home in shoes on purpose.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Seesaw Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A seesaw — one plank, two riders, and the great lesson of the playground: for me to go up, somebody goes down. Balance, weight and taking turns, bolted to a spring.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A seesaw is a long plank balanced in the middle, with a seat at each end. Push off the ground and your end rises while your friend’s end sinks — then swap.

      What is it like on the playground?

      Climb on one end, hold the handles, and bounce gently with bent knees to send your friend up. The ground rider is the engine; the high rider is the flag.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      The seesaw is physics with feelings — heavy goes down, light goes up, and the game only works with a partner. It also needs gentle legs: the best seesaw riders are smooth, not slammy.

      Say it together

      “Up… and down… up… and down! The seesaw only works when both ends agree to play — light end up, heavy end down.”

      Try this

      Two riders of very different weights? Move the small one closer to the middle — the magic balance point exists, and finding it is a real experiment.

      Quick parent note

      Seesaw rules that matter: sit facing out, hands on handles, and nobody jumps off while the other end is high. Say them like a safety cheer before the first ride.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Playground Slide Flashcard for Preschoolers

      The playground slide — ladder up, platform across, whoosh down. This one is red and yellow with a blue ladder: the classic silhouette every child recognizes from across the park.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A slide is a smooth slope with a ladder on one side. You climb, you sit, gravity does the middle part. Big slides are fast, small slides are friendly, and both end the same way: again.

      What is it like on the playground?

      The slide is the playground’s main clock — everyone queues, everyone slides, everyone lands at the bottom and looks up to check the queue again. One at a time, feet always first.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Sliding is a whole risk lesson in two seconds: the climb is effort, the top is the wobble, the ride is the reward, the landing is the proof. Repeat forty times and courage quietly compounds.

      Say it together

      “Up the blue ladder, quick sit, feet first — WHEEE, down the yellow! The slide is the playground’s promise: what goes up happily, comes down giggling.”

      Try this

      Race a different way each turn: feet first, on a grown-up’s lap (for the smallest sliders), and — the crowd favourite — spot your house from the top.

      Quick parent note

      Hot day check: metal slides cook. Touch the surface first with a hand — the hand knows before the bottom does.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Spring Rider Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A spring rider — a horse (or motorbike, or rocket) on a giant spring, ready to wobble. No pedalling, no pushing: the rider IS the engine, and the spring bounces the engine back.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A spring rider is a ride-on shape mounted on a coiled spring. It tilts every way at once, and the spring always wins — every lean comes bouncing back to centre.

      What is it like on the playground?

      Climb on from the side, grip the handles, feet on the pegs and bounce with the tummy, not just the legs. The spring counts the beats — rock along with it.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Spring riders are balance training disguised as horseback riding. The moving seat keeps the body guessing and correcting — the same wobbling-and-recovering practice as the balance beam, with a horse for company.

      Say it together

      “Hop on, hold the handles, bounce bounce bounce — the yellow horse rocks because YOU rock. Rock harder, ride wilder!”

      Try this

      Rock to a song — fast for the fast part, slow for the slow part. The spring keeps perfect time, and the song keeps the bouncing from going full storm.

      Quick parent note

      Dismount is the risky bit — the spring still moves after feet land. Teach: hands off, hop back, watch the tail.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Playground Swing Flashcard for Preschoolers

      The playground swing — two chains, one seat, endless sky. This one is a blue A-frame with a green seat: the sight that makes children drop their scooters mid-ride.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A swing is a seat hanging on chains from a frame. Push off or get pushed, then keep it going by pumping your legs — out on the way forward, tucked on the way back.

      What is it like on the playground?

      The swings are the playground’s waiting room and its throne room at once — queues full of “is it my turn yet?”, riders full of glory. Two swings, one rhythm each.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Swinging is rhythm, momentum and that delicious tummy-float all in one. Pumping your own legs is a coordination milestone — the day the pushes stop being needed is a small graduation.

      Say it together

      “Sit deep, hold tight, lean back — the swing moves when YOU move. Pump out like a frog, tuck in like a mouse.”

      Try this

      Count the pumps: how many leg pumps to touch the leaves? Then try the quiet game — swing with no pushes at all, just rhythm, as long as you can.

      Quick parent note

      Swing rules travel well: hold on with both hands, no jumping off at the top of the arc, and walk AROUND, not behind. Say it once, cheer it often.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Tunnel Flashcard for Preschoolers

      A tunnel — a crawl-through tube with a mystery in the middle. Dark for two seconds, light again, and everyone shouts. The playground’s smallest adventure, included in every visit.

      Teaching tips

      What is this?

      A tunnel is a tube big enough to crawl through. This one is blue and yellow with a bend in the middle — just enough dark to make the exit feel earned.

      What is it like on the playground?

      In the low entrance, onto hands and knees, and crawl — palms and knees taking turns, head up just enough to see the light ahead. Shout from the middle; the tube makes it hilarious.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Tunnels pack three brave things into one crawl: a small dark, a small crowd (patience if someone is ahead) and a known exit. Sensory, social and physical — in one blue tube.

      Say it together

      “Hands and knees, off we go — through the tunnel! It is dark in the middle and that is the fun part: round the bend, out the end.”

      Try this

      Peek-a-boo with the tunnel: one crawls, one waits at the end and pops in — “THERE you are!” Then swap. It never stops being funny.

      Quick parent note

      Tunnel traffic rule, same as the slide: if someone is still inside, wait for the exit wiggle. One body per tube-section keeps knees unbumped.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Help Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Help — the playground superpower that costs nothing. A hand up the step, a spade handed over, a friend walked to the gate: this card is the one that makes the playground kind.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Help means doing something useful for someone who needs it — with hands, with words or just by staying close. It starts with noticing: someone is stuck, and I could be the unsticker.

      What does it look like on the playground?

      Help is the hand up the big step, the ball fetched from under the bench, the small friend walked to the grown-up. Ask first — “do you want help?” — and then do it together.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Helping is empathy with sleeves rolled up. The helper feels important (because they are), the helped feels cared for, and the playground becomes a place people come back to.

      Say it together

      “Do you need a hand? Here — I’ll help! Helping makes the playground bigger: two people can lift what one person cannot.”

      Try this

      Play “spot the helping chance” on the way home: someone dropped a mitten, a friend’s zipper is stuck, the gate needs holding. Every spot is a chance to practise.

      Quick parent note

      Praise the noticing, not just the deed — “you SAW she was stuck” builds the muscle that finds the next chance.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Share Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Share — one ball, two hands, half each. The playground runs on sharing: shovels in the sandbox, the swing’s waiting bench, the last crisp in the packet. This card is the word that starts friendships.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Share means using something together or in turns so more than one person gets a go. It is not losing the toy — it is turning one toy into a two-person game.

      What does it look like on the playground?

      Share looks like the ball passed to the new kid, the spade offered handle-first, the sandbox corner accepted as a joint project. Timed (“two minutes each”) or mutual (“you push, I ride”) — both count.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Sharing is the entry fee of all group play — children who share get invited into more games, and the invitation is the reward. It also teaches the tick-tock of turns, which every friendship uses later.

      Say it together

      “You hold it, I hold it — we share! Sharing means the toy plays with BOTH of us, and the game gets twice as big.”

      Try this

      Split a snack deliberately: “one for you, one for me.” Then let your child do the splitting for the family. Fairness is a skill the splitter learns fastest.

      Quick parent note

      Sharing works best when the turn has an end. A visible timer or a counted turn (“ten pushes, then swap”) makes sharing feel safe instead of like losing.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Stop Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Stop — the word that halts a game before it wobbles. One hand up, feet still: stop is how the playground stays fun for everyone, and a word every child is allowed to use — and learns to respect.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Stop means end the movement, now. It is the shortest word in the set and the most powerful — it protects games, toes and feelings alike.

      What does it look like on the playground?

      Stop is the hand at the top of the slide when someone is still below, the freeze mid-tag, the “stop — my ears need quiet.” It works both ways: I can say it, and I listen when I hear it.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      A child who can stop — and who knows their stop will be respected — is safer everywhere. The word is a boundary children carry in their own mouth, which is exactly where boundaries work best.

      Say it together

      “Hand up, feet freeze — STOP! Stop is the brakes. When someone says it, we all stop and look. Then we decide what happens next.”

      Try this

      Play freeze games where STOP is the rule: dance until the song says stop, run until the whistle says stop. Practise the brake when nothing is wrong, so it works when something is.

      Quick parent note

      Never teach stop as only a grown-up word. A toddler who knows their own “stop!” gets respected sooner — and learns to give that respect back.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Take Turns Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Take turns — my go, your go, my go again. The swing queue, the slide queue, the one spade between four diggers: turns are how the playground fits everyone, and how waiting becomes a game, not a fight.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Take turns means using something one after another, so everyone gets a go. First me, then you, then me — the order can be agreed, counted or sung, but it goes round fairly.

      What does it look like on the playground?

      Turns look like the swing queue counting pushes, the seesaw swapping ends, the spade changing hands at “done!” The trick that makes it work: knowing the turn ENDS, and what happens next is mine again.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Turn-taking is the first system children run together — a tiny government of the sandbox. It teaches waiting (hard), fairness (harder) and trust that the go comes back (hardest, and most valuable).

      Say it together

      “My go… your go… my go! Turns are like a wave at the beach — it always comes back to you.”

      Try this

      Use a turn-taking song or a counted turn: “ten pushes, then swap.” The count makes the end visible, and visible ends turn waiting from misery into anticipation.

      Quick parent note

      Model losing a turn gracefully — “ah, your go, I will watch you!” Children copy the grown-up face they saw waiting.

      Teach it, step by step

      FLASHCARD · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

      Wait Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Wait — the quietest word on the playground and the hardest. Feet still, eyes on the fun: wait is the pause between “I want” and “it is my go”, and this card makes the pause feel possible.

      Teaching tips

      What does this word mean?

      Wait means staying put until it is time. Not stopping the fun — just holding your spot in it. Waiting has a shape: you can count it, sing it or watch it.

      What does it look like on the playground?

      Wait is the friend on the bench watching the swing, the feet behind the slide ladder, the spade-holder watching the digger finish. Watching counts — waiting with eyes on the game goes faster than waiting with eyes on the floor.

      Why it helps a preschooler

      Waiting is the muscle behind every turn, queue and conversation. It is genuinely hard at two, doable at three and proud at four — and the playground is the friendliest gym it will ever train in.

      Say it together

      “My body waits, my eyes watch — it is almost my go! Waiting is not doing nothing; it is watching the game until my turn arrives.”

      Try this

      Give waiting a job: count the pushes, name the colours that go by, guess how long (one hippo? two hippos?). A waiting brain with a task stops noticing the clock.

      Quick parent note

      Keep the wait honest — never promise “one more go” seven times. A wait that ends when promised teaches the child that waiting works.

      Teach it, step by step
